title: If you're struggling with something
hook: Drinking, weed, porn, vaping, gambling: a habit that came with you into Islam. You're not a fake. Here's how to keep going.

screens.text: Maybe it's drinking, weed, porn, vaping or gambling: something that came with you into Islam and hasn't left yet. If you feel like a fake, this lesson is for you. Your answers here are private.
**Struggling isn't denying.** Alcohol, drugs and gambling are forbidden [Q 5:90]. A Muslim who believes that and still slips is a believer in a hard fight, not a hypocrite.
bubbles: Saying "it's not really wrong" would be a different thing: that's denying.
Wanting to stop and falling short is struggling. Struggling Muslims are still Muslims.

screens.prompt: Struggling or denying? Sort what each person says.

items.text: "I know drinking is wrong. I keep slipping, and I hate it."
items.why: Believes it's wrong, falls short, wants to stop. That's a Muslim in a hard fight.

items.text: "Weed isn't really haram. That rule is outdated."
items.why: Calling the rule not really wrong is denying, a different thing from slipping.

items.text: "I slipped again last night. I said Astaghfirullah and prayed Fajr."
items.why: Slipping, repenting and praying the next prayer. That's exactly what struggling looks like.

items.text: "Gambling is fine for me. The rule doesn't apply to me."
items.why: Waving the rule away is the slide into denying. Keep calling it what it is.

screens.text: **The Prophet ﷺ defended a struggler.** A Companion named 'Abdullah was punished more than once for drinking. When someone cursed him, the Prophet ﷺ told him not to: this man loves Allah and His Messenger [Bukhari 6780].
bubbles: His sin was real, and so was his love for Allah. Both can be true of you, too.

screens.prompt: Dre got drunk last night. Today he feels ashamed. What should he do about today's prayers?

options.text: Pray them, once he's clear-headed, and make up any he missed
options.feedback: Yes. Prayer isn't for perfect people. Skipping it would add a second wrong to the first [IslamWeb 281668].

options.text: Skip prayer until he's been sober for a while
options.feedback: Not quite. Prayer stays due, and it's part of how he gets better. Pray as soon as he's clear-headed.

options.text: Pray while he's still drunk, so he doesn't miss it
options.feedback: Not quite. The Qur'an says not to pray intoxicated [Q 4:43]. Wait until he's clear, then pray.

screens.text: **Keep praying, no matter what.** Scholars say someone who keeps falling into a sin must keep praying. Dropping prayer doesn't make you more honest; it just adds a second wrong [IslamWeb 281668].
bubbles: And the door of **tawbah** (turning back to Allah) never closes. Repent each time, even the hundredth time.

screens.before: Allah says not to despair of His mercy: He forgives

options.feedback: Yes. All sins [Q 39:53]. The door of tawbah never closes, even the hundredth time.
Not quite. Allah forgives all sins [Q 39:53]. No habit is bigger than His mercy.
Not quite. He forgives all sins [Q 39:53]. Repent each time you slip.

screens.situation: Jordan has smoked weed most nights for years. He's tried to stop since becoming Muslim and keeps slipping. He's starting to think, "Maybe Islam isn't for people like me."

options.text: Keep praying, tell {{mentor.name}} or a counselor, and make a real plan: fewer triggers, a replacement habit, outside help
options.feedback: Yes. Faith plus a plan plus support. Long habits rarely break on willpower alone.

options.text: Quietly stop praying until he's clean, so he's not a hypocrite
options.feedback: Not quite. Prayer is his lifeline, not a reward for being clean. Struggling while praying isn't hypocrisy.

options.text: Decide it's fine since he can't stop anyway
options.feedback: Not quite. That's the slide from struggling to denying. Keep calling it what it is, and keep fighting it.

screens.text: **Get real help.** Addiction is a health problem as well as a spiritual one. The Prophet ﷺ taught that Allah made a treatment for every illness He created [Bukhari 5678]. Seeking it is part of faith.
bubbles: Talk to a doctor or counselor. In the US, the free, confidential **SAMHSA helpline is 1-800-662-4357**, any time.
Support groups help too. And {{mentor.name}} won't judge you.

screens.title: Small moves that help. Tap each one.

cards.back: Delete the contact, skip the party, get rid of the stash. Make the slip harder to reach.
Pick something for that time of day: a walk, the gym, a call, wudu and two rak'ahs.
A mentor, counselor or friend you trust. Secrets make habits stronger.
Say Astaghfirullah, make wudu, pray the next prayer, and start again. No spiral.

chips: I slipped again. Does Allah still forgive me?
How do I tell my mentor without feeling ashamed?
Can I pray if I drank earlier today?
Where can I find help near me?

screens.text: If something has a hold on you, take one step today.
steps: Pick one: save the helpline number (1-800-662-4357), tell one person, or remove one trigger
Pray your next prayer on time
screens.optional_extra: Make a short du'a in your own words: "Allah, help me let go of this."

screens.text: Struggling isn't denying. Keep praying, repent every time, and get real help. Allah's mercy is bigger than your habit.
Change usually comes slowly, with slips along the way. Every time you come back counts.

check.prompt: Someone keeps slipping into drinking. What does Islam say about their prayer?

options.text: Keep praying; dropping prayer adds a second wrong
options.feedback: Right [IslamWeb 281668]. Pray when clear-headed, and keep repenting.
Not quite. Prayer stays due and helps them heal. Quitting it adds a second wrong.

check.prompt: What's the difference between struggling and denying?

options.text: Struggling: you believe it's wrong but fall short. Denying: you say it isn't wrong
options.feedback: Right. A struggling Muslim is still a Muslim working on it.

options.text: There's no difference; any sin makes you a hypocrite
options.feedback: Not quite. The Prophet ﷺ defended a man who kept drinking but loved Allah [Bukhari 6780].

aiContext:
**Lesson facts**
- Intoxicants and gambling are forbidden [Q 5:90]. Don't pray while intoxicated; pray once clear [Q 4:43], and make up missed prayers.
- Struggling (believing it's wrong, falling short) differs from denying (rejecting the prohibition). A persistent drinker must keep praying; abandoning prayer adds a second sin [IslamWeb 281668; IslamWeb 10399].
- The Prophet ﷺ forbade cursing a man repeatedly punished for drinking, saying he loved Allah and His Messenger [Bukhari 6780].
- Repentance is always open; Allah forgives all sins [Q 39:53]. Allah created a treatment for every disease [Bukhari 5678]: seeking medical and counseling help is encouraged.
- Help: a doctor or counselor; SAMHSA National Helpline 1-800-662-4357 (free, confidential, 24/7, US); support groups; the mentor.

**Likely questions**
- *"I slipped again. Am I still Muslim?"* Yes. Struggling isn't denying. Repent, pray the next prayer, make a plan. Never imply they've left Islam.
- *"Can I pray if I drank earlier?"* Once they're clear-headed, yes, and they should. Make a fresh wudu: in the Hanafi school, being intoxicated breaks wudu. Don't pray while intoxicated [Q 4:43].
- *"Is weed / vaping / porn haram?"* Intoxicants are forbidden [Q 5:90]; porn violates lowering the gaze [Q 24:30–31]. For vaping or specific substances (e.g., prescribed medication, CBD), route details to the imam.
- *"How do I tell my mentor?"* Help them script it: "I'm struggling with something and want help." They choose how much to share.
- *"Is there a hadith about prayers not being accepted for 40 days?"* Don't cite it (not in the bank). Say: whatever the reward question, the prayer stays required, and repentance is always open.

**Escalate:** withdrawal symptoms or medical danger (doctor/911; alcohol and benzodiazepine withdrawal can be dangerous); any mention of self-harm or suicide (safety rule: 988); working in a bar, liquor store or casino (imam); prescribed medication containing alcohol or controlled substances (imam and doctor).

**Don't**
- Never shame, threaten with Hell, or use the "40 days" warning to pressure.
- Never tell someone their prayers are pointless while they're struggling, or that they should stop praying.
- Don't diagnose or give medical advice; point to professionals.
- Don't promise quick fixes or say faith alone will cure an addiction.
